rationale: Studies differ a lot in sequencing depth, 16S region and protocol, so the same genus has very different abundance distributions in each study. A pooled random forest therefore wastes splits on study artefacts. I'll convert each genus's relative abundance to a percentile within its own study (an unsupervised version of Gibbons et al. 2018 percentile normalization; it uses no labels). Values then mean "high or low for this study", which matches the within-study AUROC scoring. The classifier stays the same, so the effect of the harmonization alone is measured.

Lower gut-microbial alpha diversity is one of the most consistent IBD signals. The random forest only sees single genera, so it can't easily rebuild "how many taxa are present / how even they are." I'll add OTU Shannon, inverse Simpson, and richness at the OTU, genus and family levels. Richness is measured after seeded rarefaction to a fixed depth for each study (that study's 5th-percentile depth), so it isn't confounded by depth. Each new feature is percentile-ranked within its study, like the genera.

The current genus key keeps only the `g__` field, so every genus-unclassified OTU gets pooled into one `g__` feature regardless of family. For example, unclassified Enterobacteriaceae and unclassified Lachnospiraceae end up together, and those move in opposite directions in IBD. How much of each study classifies to genus also depends on its 16S region. This change aggregates on the full lineage prefix at every rank from phylum to genus, keeping the same within-study percentile harmonization. That keeps unclassified reads separated by their parent taxon and gives the forest family-level features (Enterobacteriaceae, Ruminococcaceae, Lachnospiraceae), which tend to be more robust across studies.

I'll keep only genera that are detected (non-zero) in at least 10% of samples in at least half of the studies, and drop the rest before percentile normalization. Genera that are rare everywhere or only show up in one study's 16S region are mostly noise or study artefacts. Removing them makes the random forest's random feature subsets more likely to include genera that are measured in every study and so can transfer across them. The filter uses no labels, and the classifier is unchanged.

Case/control ratios differ a lot between studies. Zeros also get a different percentile value in each study, because the tied-zero rank depends on how often a genus is absent there. So the pooled forest can still pick up "which study is this" and, through it, that study's case rate, which does nothing for within-study AUROC. This change weights each training sample by 1/(number of samples with its study and class), so every study counts equally with a 50/50 case/control balance. That pushes the forest's splits toward contrasts between cases and controls inside each study. It changes only how training samples are weighted: study identity is never a feature, and the features themselves don't change.

IBD dysbiosis is a broad, roughly additive shift across many genera: Faecalibacterium, Roseburia and other Clostridiales go down while Enterobacteriaceae and others go up. Fully grown random-forest trees on percentile features capture that kind of graded signal poorly. So I'll add an L2 logistic regression on the same within-study percentile features, with its regularization picked by grouped inner CV on the training fold. Its test predictions are rank-averaged with the random forest's.

The L2 logistic model currently uses within-study percentiles. Those squash all zeros into one tie and flatten fold-change size, while IBD dysbiosis is a multiplicative shift (log-scale) in many genera. I'll feed the logistic model genus CLR values (pseudocount 0.5) standardized within each study, a label-free harmonization. The random forest keeps the percentile features, so the ensemble also gets two complementary views of the data.

Add the Gevers 2014 microbial dysbiosis index — within-study z-scored CLR log-ratio of IBD-increased families (Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Veillonellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae, Gemellaceae) to IBD-decreased ones (Bacteroidales, Clostridiales/Ruminococcaceae/Lachnospiraceae, Erysipelotrichaceae) — as one prior-knowledge summary feature for both models, since neither currently sees a single aggregate of the whole dysbiotic shift.

The logistic model only sees genus CLR, and every genus-unclassified read is lumped into a single `g__` feature. That feature mixes Enterobacteriaceae with Lachnospiraceae, which move in opposite directions in IBD, and how much falls into it depends on each study's 16S region. I'll add lineage-keyed family- and order-level CLR (z-scored within study) to the L2 logistic regression only. These ranks capture the main IBD shifts (rise of Enterobacteriaceae and Pasteurellaceae, loss of Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae) and should hold up better across studies. L2 handles the correlated features from the different ranks well. The random forest stays the same, since multi-rank features hurt it in round 3.

I'm adding a third ensemble member: a shallow, heavily regularized LightGBM on the within-study z-scored genus CLR features. Its predictions are rank-averaged with the random forest and logistic regression. IBD dysbiosis includes interactions and thresholds that the additive logistic model can't capture, such as Enterobacteriaceae blooms mattering mostly once butyrate producers are depleted. Fully grown forest trees on percentiles are high-variance. Boosted shallow trees on the log-ratio view should add a complementary, lower-variance non-linear learner.

The random forest currently grows each tree until every leaf holds a single sample, on percentile features where many genera are mostly tied zeros. Each tree's vote is then close to 0/1 and depends on noise. That gives a coarse, high-variance ranking, which matters for AUROC, especially when it is rank-averaged with the smoother logistic model. This round changes only the forest: at least 3 samples per leaf and 1000 trees, so its scores are smoother and better calibrated for ranking. It still sees every genus, because dropping rare genera hurt badly in round 4.

The CLR currently uses a pseudocount of 0.5 reads on raw counts, so an undetected genus looks more depleted in a deeply sequenced sample than in a shallow one. Within-study z-scoring does not remove this within-study depth confound. I'll compute CLR on relative abundance with one pseudocount per study, 0.5 / that study's median depth. Then all non-detections in a study share the same floor whatever their depth, and the logistic model sees changes in biological log-ratios rather than sequencing effort.

The logistic model is linear in each genus's within-study z-scored CLR, so it can't express a curved dose-response such as presence/absence thresholds or saturating blooms. I'll also give it the same genus as a within-study percentile, centred and scaled per study, so each genus gets two basis functions (log-ratio scale and rank/detection scale). L2 can then fit a bent per-genus effect while the model stays additive and well regularized. The random forest is unchanged.

The two models' predictions are currently rank-averaged over the whole pooled test set. The metric is within-study AUROC, so pooled ranks are the wrong scale to combine on. If a study's random forest scores all land in a narrow band of pooled ranks (its case rate or depth differs from the other studies), that model barely affects the ordering inside that study, and the forest–logistic balance ends up varying arbitrarily from study to study. I'll convert each model's test predictions to percentile ranks within each test study (using `meta_test` study only to harmonize outputs, never as a predictor) before averaging. Both models then carry equal weight within every study, which is exactly where scoring happens.

The logistic model's L2 strength is currently tuned by inner CV that scores pooled AUROC. Pooled AUROC also rewards separating studies with different case rates, while the real score is within-study AUROC. I'll choose C by inner-CV AUROC computed within each study and averaged across studies. That matches the harness metric, and the training-set study labels are used only to group the scoring, never as a feature.

This adds a third ensemble member, a beta-diversity nearest-neighbour score. For each test sample it computes the mean Aitchison distance (Euclidean on raw genus CLR) to its k nearest training controls minus the same distance to its k nearest training cases. Neighbours come only from training samples of the same study, because 16S region and protocol make cross-study distances meaningless. IBD samples sit apart from controls in ordination space, and this whole-community similarity view is something neither the per-genus forest nor the additive logistic model captures. Study is used only to restrict which distances get compared, and predictions are still ranked within study before averaging.

The random forest and the logistic model are currently given a fixed 50/50 weight. Earlier rounds suggest the CLR logistic model is the stronger of the two: every round that added a third member or diluted it scored lower. This change picks the blend weight by grouped inner CV on the training fold. It scores within-study AUROC on out-of-fold predictions, ranked within study, to match the harness metric, and shrinks the chosen weight halfway toward 0.5 so inner-CV noise has less effect.

The logistic model's features are genus CLR values z-scored within each study. A genus that is detected in only a few samples of a study gets z-scores of 10 or more for those samples, so a single sporadic detection can dominate that sample's L2-logistic score and add noise to the within-study ranking. I'll clip the within-study z-scored CLR to [-3, 3] so rare blooms still register as strongly high but no longer act as outliers with huge leverage. This changes only the logistic model's inputs; the random forest's percentile features stay the same.

Some subjects contribute several stool samples, and right now both models weight every sample equally. The models can therefore learn those subjects' personal microbiome quirks instead of the IBD signal, which the grouped CV then penalises. I'll weight each training sample by 1/(number of samples from that subject), taken from `ctx["groups_train"]` and rescaled to a mean of 1, in both the random forest and the CV-tuned L2 logistic regression. Each person then counts once. If every subject has only one sample, all weights are 1 and nothing changes.

I'm replacing the random forest with an ExtraTrees ensemble (1000 trees) on the same within-study percentile genus features. Most genera are tied zeros within each study, so the forest's best-split trees chase noise and give spiky, high-variance rankings. ExtraTrees picks split thresholds at random, which averages over many cut-points and should give a smoother, lower-variance within-study ordering to rank-average with the CLR logistic model. This change has not been run yet, so its Dev score is unknown.
